title: Build a contract renewal tracker
description: A system that scans your contract repository on a schedule and drafts a memo before any renewal or termination deadline slips by.

pull.title: Pull
pull.content: Downloading the latest changes from GitHub to your computer so your local copy is up to date. Claude pulls before starting work to make sure it's building on the newest version, not an old one.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

slack.title: Slack
slack.content: The team messaging app most companies run on. In Level 2, students connect Slack to their AI tools to trigger workflows from messages, post AI-generated updates to channels, or summarize threads automatically.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

notion.title: Notion
notion.content: An all-in-one workspace for docs, wikis, databases, and project tracking. Used heavily across the AI Builder program as a destination for AI-generated content and as a connected app in Level 2 automations.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

read-only.title: Read-only
read-only.content: The first rung of the trust gradient: the agent can see your inbox, calendar, or docs but can't change anything. The default starting state for every new tool connection. Tiny blast radius, fast to ship, and confirms the read side works before you graduate the write side.

repository.title: Repository (Repo)
repository.content: A project folder tracked by Git. Your GitHub repo is where Claude stores your code and files. When Claude 'pushes to GitHub,' it's sending changes from your computer to the online repo.

children.text: A renewal date lapses because nobody rechecked the folder it sits in. Research from World Commerce & Contracting, [as reported by Juro](https://juro.com/learn/contract-value-leakage), puts revenue lost to poor contract management, including missed renewals and untracked obligations, at roughly 9% of annual revenue, with top-performing organizations holding that leakage to about 3% and the weakest losing 15-20% of a contract's value over its lifetime.
Nearly half of organizations fail to track at least some of their contracts, per the same research. A scheduled scan is built to close exactly that gap.

Run it as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) against a contract export, a saved skill, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that checks the [repository](#tooltip-repository) weekly and messages owners directly. Every version stays [read-only](#tooltip-read-only) against your contract system.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming where your contracts live, your notice-window rules, what the memo needs to include, and who receives it.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that scans our contract repository for upcoming renewal and termination-notice dates and drafts a memo before anything lapses. Ask me questions, one at a time, about where our contracts actually live today, what notice windows matter for our contract types, who owns each contract relationship, and what the memo needs to include for someone to act on it. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview surfaces the notice-window and ownership questions you'd otherwise discover only after a deadline passes, and the scope document becomes the brief for every review after it.

items: Where your contract repository lives, and whether the dates and owners in it are reliable enough to scan.
Who owns each contract relationship in practice, not just on paper.
Your default posture on auto-renewal, so the system knows what no action taken means.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather your contract repository (Ironclad, DocuSign CLM, or a structured shared drive), your calendar or task tool (Google Calendar, [Notion](#tooltip-notion), Asana), and your team chat ([Slack](#tooltip-slack), Teams). The paste-in version needs none.
**Create.** Build your system and test it on a real export of your contract repository. The prompt below is an example. Your scope document gives a version for your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Scan [our contract repository] for any contract with a renewal, termination-notice, or expiration date falling within the next 90 days, and draft a short memo for each one.

Context: Contracts live in [CLM/shared drive/folder structure]. Contract owners are listed in [location, e.g. a metadata field or a separate roster]. Our default posture on auto-renewal is [renew unless flagged/require active renewal].

Rules:
- Flag every contract crossing the 90-, 60-, and 30-day thresholds, not just the ones expiring soonest.
- Pull the actual notice-period language from each contract rather than assuming a standard window.
- Name the specific owner responsible for the decision in every memo.
- State clearly whether the contract auto-renews by default and the deadline to opt out.
- Output format: one memo per contract with contract name, key dates, owner, auto-renewal status, and a recommended action.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: naming the exact thresholds and requiring the real notice-period language keeps the memo tied to what each contract says instead of a standard-window guess.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Every crossing threshold flagged, an owner named, auto-renewal status stated in plain terms?
**Feedback.** Correct the rules. Fold each fix ("that owner field is stale, [pull](#tooltip-pull) from the roster instead") straight into the prompt.

items: Build a rolling dashboard of every contract's next key date instead of only surfacing the urgent ones.
Add a clause-extraction pass that pulls notice-period language automatically for contracts where it isn't tagged.
Extend the tracker to flag price-escalation clauses, not just dates.
Add an escalation rule when an owner hasn't acted within a set window before the deadline.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric), not a feel check. Have your AI chat draft the rubric and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each renewal memo, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for review date, contracts flagged, owner notified, action taken, and actual outcome (renewed, terminated, or missed). Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the outcome column is what catches a memo that looked right but still reached the wrong person too late.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Each entry takes a minute. Note the date, which rubric checks passed or failed, and what you changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the system passes the rubric a few cycles straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write the skill for you, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One failure mode. A tracker is only as reliable as the metadata behind it. If dates or owners are wrong in the source repository, the memo looks authoritative while pointing at the wrong deadline. Spot-check the underlying data before trusting the schedule.
